title: Neural Basis of Symbolic and Non-Symbolic Quantity Processing in Human Brain with fMRI
author: Altınok, Vatansever, et al.
materials: Brain images can be analyzed with different kinds of tools or software. Furthermore, applications for these analyses may vary between researchers as well as among neuroimaging laboratories. To gain a full and better perspective about these practices of the neuroimaging analysis, you may check Nichols et al. (2017). Here, we share our approach to analyze the neural activations rather than a standard guideline for neuroimaging analysis. In this paper you will find a pipeline of analysis that is used in our fMRI studies of numerical cognition in children with dyscalculia (Üstün et al., 2021) and people at different developmental stages (Vatansever et al., 2020). In the scope of this protocol, the event-related functional images will be processed using SPM12 software, which needs MATLAB software to run.

steps.title: Prepare computing environment
steps.instruction: Ensure a 64‑bit computer with at least 16 GB RAM and an Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU E5‑1650 v4 @ 3.60 GHz is available. Approximate processing times are 10 min for behavioral analysis, 30 min per participant for fMRI first‑ and second‑level analysis, and 1 h per participant for ROI analysis.

steps.title: Set up analysis software
steps.instruction: Install MATLAB and the SPM12 toolbox (which runs inside MATLAB). Also install the MarsBaR toolbox for ROI work.

steps.title: Obtain behavioral parameters
steps.instruction: After each fMRI session, retrieve the two behavioral outputs generated by the paradigm code: (1) response time and (2) percentage of correct responses.

steps.title: Analyze behavioral data
steps.instruction: Perform a repeated‑measures ANOVA on the behavioral data with the factors numerosity, difficulty, and group to test for interactions.

steps.title: Specify first‑level GLM
steps.instruction: For each participant, create a first‑level design matrix in SPM12 that includes four experimental conditions (symbolic‑easy, symbolic‑difficult, non‑symbolic‑easy, non‑symbolic‑difficult) and six motion parameters as regressors of no interest, plus a session mean. Set the high‑pass filter to the default 128 s.

substeps.instruction: Enter the output folder path in the Directory field.
In Timing parameters, input the scanning parameters of the acquisition.
Under Data & Design → Scans, load the pre‑processed fMRI data for the first run.
In Condition, define the four conditions listed above.
Enter the trial onsets for each condition in the Onsets column.
Load the head‑movement parameters for the first run into Multiple regressors.
Repeat the Scans, Conditions, Onsets, and Multiple regressors sections for the remaining three runs, keeping the settings identical.
In the Factorial Design section, define two factors (Number and Difficulty) each with two levels.

steps.title: Estimate first‑level model
steps.instruction: Open the Estimate module in SPM, load the SPM.mat file generated by the specification step, and run the batch to estimate beta values and create contrast images for each condition.

steps.title: Batch first‑level across participants
steps.instruction: Load the first‑level batch in SPM’s Batch Editor, view the generated .m code (Batch → View → Show .m Code), edit the script to loop over all participants, and execute it to process every subject automatically.

steps.title: Run second‑level ANOVA
steps.instruction: Perform a three‑way repeated‑measures ANOVA using SPM12’s Flexible Factorial design with the factors: (1) Number (symbolic vs. non‑symbolic), (2) Difficulty (easy vs. difficult), and (3) Group (group 1 vs. group 2). If no grouping factor is present, use a two‑way ANOVA (Number × Difficulty). For studies including participants with dyscalculia, add overall IQ, verbal IQ, and age as covariates.

steps.title: Estimate second‑level model
steps.instruction: Open the Estimate section on the SPM menu, load the second‑level SPM.mat file, and run the batch to compute the ANOVA statistics.

steps.title: Display results and apply thresholds
steps.instruction: In SPM, click Results, load the second‑level SPM.mat file, and view the statistical maps. Run a Monte Carlo simulation with 10 000 iterations for a voxel‑wise threshold of p < 0.001 (Slotnick, 2017). The simulation will provide the cluster‑extent threshold k ≥ voxels required for a corrected cluster‑level significance of p < 0.05.

steps.title: Create ROIs with MarsBaR
steps.instruction: Define regions of interest from all interaction‑effect clusters using MarsBaR:

substeps.instruction: Accept the default options to display the results.
In the SPM input window, click Write ROI(s) and choose Write all clusters.
Specify a folder; MarsBaR will name each ROI file with its coordinates.

steps.title: Extract ROI signal change
steps.instruction: Use MarsBaR to extract the mean percent signal change for each ROI and each participant.

steps.title: Interpret ROI data
steps.instruction: Visually inspect the extracted mean percent signal change values to assess the direction of effects; avoid further statistical testing on these ROI data to prevent circularity.

description: The protocol below describes the instructional steps to examine neural underpinnings of numerosity comparison at various difficulty levels (easy and difficult) using fMRI.
